record.paper_title: Billiard dynamics: A survey with the emphasis on open problems
record.original_question: Does every polygonal billiard table have at least one periodic billiard orbit?

evidence.quote: Задача 10. Всякий ли многоугольник имеет периодическую орбиту?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a billiard inside a polygon P in the Euclidean plane: a point particle moves in straight lines inside P at unit speed, and upon hitting a side of P (away from a vertex) it reflects so that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; trajectories that hit a vertex are left undefined. A billiard trajectory is called periodic if, after finitely many reflections, the particle returns to its initial position with its initial direction.

Question: Does every polygon P (in particular, every triangle) admit at least one periodic billiard trajectory?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is known to be open in general. Periodic orbits are known to exist for rational polygons (by Masur), for acute and right triangles (Fagnano-type), and—by Schwartz's computer-assisted work—for every obtuse triangle whose largest angle is at most 100°. The general case (in particular, obtuse triangles with angle exceeding ~112.5°, and arbitrary irrational polygons) remains unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Obtuse Triangular Billiards II: 100 Degrees Worth of Periodic Trajectories
status_evidence.snippet: Every obtuse triangle with largest angle at most 100 degrees has a periodic billiard path.
status_evidence.claim: Schwartz proved existence of periodic orbits for obtuse triangles up to 100°, but the general problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Survey Lecture on Billiards (Schwartz, ICM)
status_evidence.snippet: It is an outstanding open problem whether every polygonal billiard has a periodic orbit.
status_evidence.claim: The existence of a periodic orbit in every polygonal billiard is an outstanding open problem.
